tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup was hot, spicy, and fragrant.
She likes hiking mountain trails and to swim in cold lakes.
Volunteers must arrive early, sign the register, and wearing a badge.
The guide was both patient and she explained every landmark.
He enjoys reading crime novels, sketching street scenes, and baking bread.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The soup was hot, spicy, and fragrant.**

Three adjectives — hot, spicy, and fragrant — share the same slot after was. Each item is the same part of speech, so the list never jumps into a verb or a clause. That matching shape is exactly what parallel structure asks for after a linking verb.

Matching adjectives after was keep every item in one slot, so the wording is **true**.
**B) She likes hiking mountain trails and to swim in cold lakes.**

After likes, the first object is hiking (a gerund), but the second is to swim (an infinitive). Both ideas are activities she enjoys, yet the forms do not match. Keep the pair in matching -ing shapes: hiking… and swimming….

**Trap:** Mixing a gerund with a to-infinitive after likes is a classic exam near-miss because both forms can name activities.

Gerund and infinitive clash after likes, so the line is **false** — "She likes hiking mountain trails and swimming in cold lakes."
**C) Volunteers must arrive early, sign the register, and wearing a badge.**

Must governs a series of bare infinitives: arrive and sign fit that pattern, but wearing does not. Wearing is a participle, so the shared modal loses its bare-form chain. After must, every branch needs the same bare verb — wear a badge, not wearing a badge.

**Trap:** The last item looks like another duty, but the -ing ending quietly breaks the must + bare-verb series.

Must governs bare verbs only, so wearing is **false** — "…arrive early, sign the register, and wear a badge."
**D) The guide was both patient and she explained every landmark.**

Both…and must join two matching structures, but patient is an adjective while she explained every landmark is a full clause. Related ideas are not enough; the grammatical clothes on each half must match. Rewrite the second half as an adjective or adjective phrase so both sides balance.

**Trap:** Both…and often tricks writers into linking a short adjective to a whole sentence that only feels related.

Both…and can’t join an adjective to a clause, so this is **false** — "The guide was both patient and clear."
**E) He enjoys reading crime novels, sketching street scenes, and baking bread.**

Enjoys takes three gerund phrases — reading…, sketching…, and baking… — in the same -ing shape. Each hobby is packed as an -ing activity, with no sudden switch into a to-infinitive. That matching pattern is the clean frame for lists of things someone enjoys.

Three matching -ing hobbies after enjoys fit the frame, so the sentence is **true**.
highlights: reading crime novels, sketching street scenes, and baking
tasks.solution_overview:
Five everyday sentences about food, hobbies, and volunteering — each built around a list or a paired correlative. Your job is to decide whether the pieces dressed the same way.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Parallel structure means every item in a list, or each half of a correlative such as both…and, must share the same grammatical shape. Watch adjectives after a linking verb, gerunds after likes/enjoys, bare forms after must, and the two sides of both…and.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the form of the first item, then check that every later item can wear the same grammatical clothes. One mismatched ending is enough to mark the sentence false, even when the meaning is clear.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The playlist mixed jazz standards, folk ballads, and indie rock.
Their weekend plan was to visit museums, trying new cafés, and walk along the river.
Maya is good at repairing bikes but weak in organising toolkits.
The course aims to build stamina, improve balance, and boosting confidence.
Tom likes watering the garden and pruning the hedges.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The playlist mixed jazz standards, folk ballads, and indie rock.**

Mixed is followed by three noun phrases: jazz standards, folk ballads, and indie rock. Every object is the same kind of noun phrase, so the playlist list stays balanced. Noun lists after a transitive verb are parallel when each item could swap places without changing form.

Jazz, folk, and indie rock all sit as noun objects after mixed, so the playlist wording is **true**.
**B) Their weekend plan was to visit museums, trying new cafés, and walk along the river.**

The plan opens with to visit and should continue as a bare-infinitive series after that to. Trying breaks the chain because it is a gerund, while walk later returns to bare form. Keep visit, try, and walk — not trying — once the infinitive frame has started.

**Trap:** A middle -ing form often looks like another activity on the weekend list, but it snaps the to + infinitive series.

A middle gerund snaps the to + infinitive plan, so the line is **false** — "…to visit museums, try new cafés, and walk along the river."
**C) Maya is good at repairing bikes but weak in organising toolkits.**

Each side uses an adjective plus a preposition-plus-gerund frame: good at repairing… but weak in organising…. The prepositions differ (at / in), yet both halves keep the same preposition + gerund pattern. That matching scaffold is what makes the comparison parallel.

Good at… and weak in… both wear preposition-plus-gerund frames, so the comparison is **true**.
**D) The course aims to build stamina, improve balance, and boosting confidence.**

Aims to sets up bare infinitives: build and improve fit, but boosting is a gerund. The last goal must wear the same bare form after to. Finish with boost confidence so the aims-to series never changes clothes mid-list.

**Trap:** Boosting confidence sounds like a natural course aim, which is why the gerund is an easy near-miss after build and improve.

Aims to needs bare infinitives throughout, so boosting is **false** — "…to build stamina, improve balance, and boost confidence."
**E) Tom likes watering the garden and pruning the hedges.**

Likes takes two gerund phrases — watering the garden and pruning the hedges — in matching -ing form. Nothing slips into a to-infinitive on the second side. That is the expected pattern when one verb introduces two activities someone enjoys.

Two matching gerunds after likes name the chores cleanly, so the pair is **true**.
highlights: jazz standards, folk ballads, and indie rock
tasks.solution_overview:
A short set mixing noun lists, infinitive plans, skill comparisons, and course aims. Scan each series for one item that quietly changes grammatical shape.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Focus on parallel noun objects after mixed, infinitive chains after was to, adjective + preposition + gerund pairs in comparisons, and bare infinitives after aims to. The false marks almost always hide in the last item of the series.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read the list left to right and freeze the opening pattern. If the last branch cannot swap places with the first without changing structure, mark the sentence false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The leaflet explains how to book a seat, how to print a ticket, and how to find the platform.
Ideal flatmates should be tidy, considerate, and pay rent on time.
The club both renovated the court and installed new lights.
Our goals are finishing homework early, sleeping enough, and to exercise daily.
The judge asked whether the answers were complete, accurate, and fair.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The leaflet explains how to book a seat, how to print a ticket, and how to find the platform.**

Explains how to introduces three matching how to phrases: book a seat, print a ticket, and find the platform. Repeating how to before each step keeps the shared instructional frame unmistakable. The leaflet therefore never mixes a how-phrase with a bare noun or a stray clause.

Repeating how to before each step mirrors the leaflet’s frame, so the wording is **true**.
**B) Ideal flatmates should be tidy, considerate, and pay rent on time.**

Tidy and considerate are adjectives after should be, but pay rent on time is a verb phrase. The list cannot mix adjective qualities with a sudden duty in bare-verb form. Either write three adjectives, or rewrite the whole list as verbs if that is the intended idea.

**Trap:** Pay rent on time feels like another flatmate virtue, so the part-of-speech switch is easy to miss.

An adjective chain can’t finish as a bare verb, so this is **false** — "…tidy, considerate, and punctual with rent."
**C) The club both renovated the court and installed new lights.**

Both…and links renovated the court and installed new lights — two matching past-tense verb phrases. Each half of the correlative wears the same finite-verb clothes. That is the clean pattern when a club completed two parallel upgrades.

Both…and joins two matching past-tense upgrades, so the correlative is **true**.
**D) Our goals are finishing homework early, sleeping enough, and to exercise daily.**

Finishing and sleeping are gerunds after are, but to exercise is an infinitive. Goal lists need one shared form all the way through. Keep the -ing series: finishing…, sleeping…, and exercising….

**Trap:** To exercise daily looks like a tidy goal, which is why an infinitive often sneaks into a gerund goal list.

Goal lists after are can’t mix gerunds with an infinitive, so the line is **false** — "…finishing homework early, sleeping enough, and exercising daily."
**E) The judge asked whether the answers were complete, accurate, and fair.**

Were is followed by three adjectives — complete, accurate, and fair — in one continuous chain. After a linking verb, every item in that checklist should stay an adjective. Nothing drifts into a clause or a verb phrase at the end.

Complete, accurate, and fair stay adjectives after were, so the checklist is **true**.
highlights: how to book a seat, how to print a ticket, and how to find
both renovated the court and installed
tasks.solution_overview:
Instructions, flatmate traits, club upgrades, personal goals, and a judge's checklist — all as A–E lists. Keep the opening pattern alive through the last item.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch for matching how to phrases, adjective lists that suddenly become verbs, both…and with matching verb phrases, goals written as mixed gerunds and infinitives, and clean adjective chains after were.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask what grammatical template the sentence starts with — how to…, adjective…, past-tense verb…, gerund… — then force every later branch to copy it. Reject any sentence that switches mid-list.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The film was long, confusing, and it bored the audience.
She not only packed the tent but also checked the weather forecast.
Passengers must queue calmly, show their tickets, and to board in groups.
Cooking requires patience, practice, and a sharp knife.
He spends weekends repairing bikes, coaching juniors, and to race himself.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The film was long, confusing, and it bored the audience.**

Long and confusing are adjectives after was, but it bored the audience is a full clause. Adjective lists cannot finish as independent sentences just because the ideas relate. Use a third adjective so every item sits in the same slot after was.

**Trap:** A trailing it-clause feels like a natural film complaint, which hides the break from adjective to clause.

An adjective list can’t end as an it-clause, so this is **false** — "The film was long, confusing, and dull."
**B) She not only packed the tent but also checked the weather forecast.**

Not only…but also joins packed the tent and checked the weather forecast — two matching past-tense verb phrases. Each half of the correlative keeps the same finite-verb shape. That matching structure is what makes the packing checklist parallel.

Not only…but also balances two past-tense packing acts, so the wording is **true**.
**C) Passengers must queue calmly, show their tickets, and to board in groups.**

Must takes bare infinitives: queue and show fit, but to board brings an unwanted to. Once the modal owns the series, every later verb must stay bare. Board in groups — not to board — keeps the shared must pattern intact.

**Trap:** To board looks grammatical in isolation, which is why an extra to often sneaks into a must list.

Must takes bare verbs, so the extra to before board is **false** — "…queue calmly, show their tickets, and board in groups."
**D) Cooking requires patience, practice, and a sharp knife.**

Requires is followed by three noun phrases: patience, practice, and a sharp knife. Concrete tools and abstract needs can share one noun-list slot after requires. Nothing switches mid-list into a clause or an infinitive.

Patience, practice, and a sharp knife share one noun slot after requires, so the sentence is **true**.
**E) He spends weekends repairing bikes, coaching juniors, and to race himself.**

Spending weekends with hobbies should keep -ing forms: repairing and coaching fit, but to race does not. An infinitive in the last slot breaks the gerund series after spends weekends. Use racing himself so every weekend activity stays an -ing phrase.

**Trap:** To race himself names a real hobby, so the infinitive is a near-miss inside an otherwise -ing list.

Weekend hobbies after spends need -ing forms, so to race is **false** — "…repairing bikes, coaching juniors, and racing himself."
highlights: not only packed the tent but also checked
patience, practice, and a sharp knife
tasks.solution_overview:
Warm-up items mixing film reviews, packing correlatives, boarding instructions, cooking needs, and weekend hobbies. Name the first item's form before you trust the ending.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The usual traps are adjective lists that finish as clauses, not only…but also with matching verb phrases, shared must with a stray to-infinitive, noun objects after requires, and gerund series broken by an infinitive.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Label item one (adjective, bare infinitive after must, gerund, noun), then reject any ending that cannot wear those same clothes. Correlatives need matching halves, not just related ideas.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The hike was rewarding because of the views, because of the fresh air, and the group was cheerful.
Either leave your bags in the locker or carry them with you at all times.
The recipe calls for chopping the onions, frying the spices, and to simmer the sauce.
Spectators clapped loudly, whistled in rhythm, and waved homemade banners.
She wants a laptop that is light, that is quiet, and affordable.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The hike was rewarding because of the views, because of the fresh air, and the group was cheerful.**

Two reasons open as because of + noun phrases, but the group was cheerful is an independent clause. Once because of sets the frame, every later reason should stay a noun phrase under that same marker. Rewrite the last reason so it still hangs from because of, not as a freestanding clause.

**Trap:** A cheerful-group clause feels like another good reason for the hike, which hides the frame switch.

Because of sets a noun-phrase frame the closing clause leaves, so the line is **false** — "…because of the views, because of the fresh air, and because of the cheerful group."
**B) Either leave your bags in the locker or carry them with you at all times.**

Either…or joins leave your bags… and carry them… — two matching bare infinitives with one shared subject. Each half keeps the same verb form and does not invent a new subject. That is the clean pattern for alternative instructions under either…or.

Either…or pairs two bare infinitives with one subject, so the instruction is **true**.
**C) The recipe calls for chopping the onions, frying the spices, and to simmer the sauce.**

Calls for takes gerund objects: chopping and frying fit, but to simmer is an infinitive. Recipe sequences after calls for must stay in -ing form through the last step. Finish with simmering the sauce so the gerund list never changes shape.

**Trap:** To simmer the sauce sounds like a natural recipe step, so the infinitive is a near-miss after two gerunds.

Calls for wants gerunds through the last step, so to simmer is **false** — "…chopping the onions, frying the spices, and simmering the sauce."
**D) Spectators clapped loudly, whistled in rhythm, and waved homemade banners.**

Three past-tense verb phrases — clapped, whistled, and waved — share one subject and one tense. Crowd actions stay parallel when every verb could swap places without changing form. Nothing drifts into a different tense or a sudden clause at the end.

Clapped, whistled, and waved keep one past-tense shape, so the crowd list is **true**.
**E) She wants a laptop that is light, that is quiet, and affordable.**

Two relative modifiers open with that is, but affordable stands alone without that marker. Either repeat that is before the last adjective, or drop that is before all three and list them as a plain chain. Partial repetition of a relative frame is what breaks the laptop wish-list.

**Trap:** Affordable looks fine as a third quality, which is why missing that is is easy to overlook.

Partial that is leaves the last quality bare, so this is **false** — "…that is light, that is quiet, and that is affordable."
highlights: clapped loudly, whistled in rhythm, and waved
tasks.solution_overview:
Reasons for a hike, locker instructions, a recipe sequence, a lively crowd, and a laptop wish-list. Repeated subordinators and correlatives fail when the last branch changes shape.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Check that because of, either…or, calls for + gerund, past-tense verb lists, and that is relatives appear consistently across every branch — or rewrite the whole list in one frame.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If a marker appears twice, the third branch almost always needs it too. Read the list aloud; an abrupt change of rhythm usually signals a break in form.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: By stretching carefully, by drinking water, and by resting between sets, he avoided injury.
The museum tour was informative, interactive, and we learned about local pottery.
Parents asked the coach to explain the drills, to demonstrate each move, and feedback after practice.
Neither the rain nor the wind stopped the outdoor market.
Her weekend routine involves cycling to the bakery, collecting the newspaper, and she waters the plants.
tactical_explanations:
**A) By stretching carefully, by drinking water, and by resting between sets, he avoided injury.**

Three matching by + gerund phrases — stretching, drinking, resting — list the means that avoided injury. Repeating by before each gerund keeps the causal scaffold audible and balanced. That is the clean pattern for a means list built on by + -ing.

Three by + gerund means phrases match end to end, so the wording is **true**.
**B) The museum tour was informative, interactive, and we learned about local pottery.**

Informative and interactive are adjectives after was, but we learned about local pottery is a clause. Tour descriptions cannot finish as freestanding sentences inside an adjective chain. Use a third adjective so every item remains in the same slot after was.

**Trap:** A trailing we-learned clause feels like extra praise for the tour, which hides the adjective-to-clause break.

Tour adjectives can’t finish as a we-learned clause, so the line is **false** — "The museum tour was informative, interactive, and memorable."
**C) Parents asked the coach to explain the drills, to demonstrate each move, and feedback after practice.**

Asked…to sets an infinitive series: to explain and to demonstrate fit, but feedback after practice is a bare noun. The parents' request must keep to + verb on every branch. Add to give feedback after practice so the infinitive series stays intact.

**Trap:** Feedback after practice names a real request and therefore looks parallel until you notice the missing to + verb.

Asked…to needs to + verb on every branch, so bare feedback is **false** — "…to explain the drills, to demonstrate each move, and to give feedback after practice."
**D) Neither the rain nor the wind stopped the outdoor market.**

Neither…nor joins the rain and the wind — two matching noun phrases as a compound subject. Both sides stay in the same category: noun + noun, not noun + clause. That matching pair is exactly what the correlative needs.

Neither…nor balances rain and wind as matching nouns, so the correlative is **true**.
**E) Her weekend routine involves cycling to the bakery, collecting the newspaper, and she waters the plants.**

Involves takes gerund objects: cycling and collecting fit, but she waters the plants is an independent clause. Weekend-routine lists after involves must stay gerunds through the last chore. Use watering the plants so every item wears the same -ing clothes.

**Trap:** A full she-waters clause feels like another routine detail, which is why the break from gerund to clause is sneaky.

Involves takes gerunds, so a freestanding she-waters clause is **false** — "…cycling to the bakery, collecting the newspaper, and watering the plants."
highlights: By stretching carefully, by drinking water, and by resting
Neither the rain nor the wind
tasks.solution_overview:
Means lists with by + gerund, museum descriptions, coach requests, weather correlatives, and weekend routines. Trailing clauses after adjective or gerund pairs are the usual false marks.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Clean patterns here are by + gerund means lists and neither…nor with matching nouns. Dirty patterns are adjective pairs that finish as clauses, infinitive series that end as bare nouns, and gerund pairs that end as independent clauses.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat the first branch as a template. If the last item is a new clause or a different part of speech, mark false — meaning alone never rescues a broken list.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The role of team captain involves motivating players, planning practices, and attendance at matches.
We are looking for someone who can think clearly, act calmly, and speak kindly.
The prize will be used both to buy new books and decorating the reading corner.
His strengths are curiosity, humour, and solving puzzles quickly.
The committee voted to approve the mural, to hire a local artist, and to schedule the unveiling.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The role of team captain involves motivating players, planning practices, and attendance at matches.**

Involves opens with gerunds — motivating and planning — but attendance at matches is a plain noun phrase. Captain duties after involves should stay -ing actions, not abstract nouns mixed into the series. Use attending matches so every duty matches the gerund pattern.

**Trap:** Attendance at matches names a real duty and therefore looks parallel until the noun form breaks the -ing list.

Captain duties after involves should stay -ing, so attendance is **false** — "…motivating players, planning practices, and attending matches."
**B) We are looking for someone who can think clearly, act calmly, and speak kindly.**

Can governs three bare infinitives — think, act, and speak — with matching -ly adverbs. Shared modals demand the same bare verb form on every branch. Nothing sneaks in a to-infinitive or a sudden clause at the end.

Can governs think, act, and speak as bare infinitives, so the wording is **true**.
**C) The prize will be used both to buy new books and decorating the reading corner.**

Both…and joins to buy new books (an infinitive) to decorating the reading corner (a gerund). Correlative halves must wear the same form, not merely related spending ideas. Match both sides as infinitives or both as gerunds.

**Trap:** Decorating the reading corner sounds like a twin use of the prize, so the gerund/infinitive clash is a classic trap.

Both…and can’t mix an infinitive with a gerund, so the prize use is **false** — "both to buy… and to decorate…" or "both buying… and decorating…."
**D) His strengths are curiosity, humour, and solving puzzles quickly.**

Curiosity and humour are nouns after are, but solving puzzles quickly is a gerund phrase. Strength lists need one shared category through every item. Turn the last item into a noun phrase so all three strengths match.

**Trap:** A gerund skill often feels like another personal strength beside two abstract nouns — that mix is the near-miss.

Strengths after are need matching nouns, so solving puzzles is **false** — "…curiosity, humour, and quick puzzle-solving."
**E) The committee voted to approve the mural, to hire a local artist, and to schedule the unveiling.**

Voted to introduces three infinitives — approve, hire, and schedule — with to repeated before each. Repeating to is optional, but here it keeps equal weight on every committee action. The mural vote therefore never mixes infinitives with nouns or gerunds.

Voted to + three equal infinitives keeps the mural actions parallel, so the sentence is **true**.
highlights: think clearly, act calmly, and speak
both to buy new books and decorating
to approve the mural, to hire
tasks.solution_overview:
Captain duties, calm applicants, reading-corner prizes, personal strengths, and mural votes. Duty lists and both…and often hide mixed nouns, gerunds, and infinitives.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Convert every item into the same type before you judge: gerund objects after involves, bare infinitives after can, matching infinitives or gerunds after both…and, all nouns after are, and infinitives after voted to.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Say the opening type out loud — gerund, bare verb, noun, to-infinitive — then force every later item to match. If you cannot swap item three with item one, the sentence is false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The campaign was effective in raising awareness, in recruiting helpers, and donations increased.
Applicants must either enclose a sketchbook or they submit a link to an online gallery.
The chef is known for bold flavours, neat plating, and generous portions.
We aim not only to finish the trail but also the photos for the blog.
The workshop taught participants to define goals, to map their route, and to pack a first-aid kit.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The campaign was effective in raising awareness, in recruiting helpers, and donations increased.**

Two results open as in + gerund phrases, but donations increased is an independent clause. Once effective in sets a preposition-plus-gerund frame, every later result should stay inside that frame. Keep the last branch as in + gerund rather than a freestanding clause.

**Trap:** A results clause about donations feels thematic, which hides the switch away from in + gerund.

Effective in + gerund can’t end as a donations clause, so this is **false** — "…in raising awareness, in recruiting helpers, and in increasing donations."
**B) Applicants must either enclose a sketchbook or they submit a link to an online gallery.**

Either…or joins enclose a sketchbook (bare infinitive after must) to they submit a link (full clause with a new subject). Correlative alternatives need the same subject and the same verb form on both sides. Drop the new they and keep submit as a bare infinitive under must either…or.

**Trap:** A full they-submit clause looks like a complete alternative, so the subject switch is a sharp exam trap.

Either…or under must can’t invent a new they-subject, so the line is **false** — "…either enclose a sketchbook or submit a link to an online gallery."
**C) The chef is known for bold flavours, neat plating, and generous portions.**

Known for takes three noun phrases: bold flavours, neat plating, and generous portions. After for, noun lists are usually the safest parallel choice for reputation traits. Nothing drifts into a clause or an infinitive at the end.

Known for takes three noun traits in one slot, so the reputation list is **true**.
**D) We aim not only to finish the trail but also the photos for the blog.**

Not only…but also joins to finish the trail (infinitive) to the photos for the blog (bare noun). Both halves of the correlative must share the same structure, including the to if the first half has it. Match the second half as an infinitive as well.

**Trap:** The photos for the blog is a related blog chore, which makes the missing to easy to overlook.

Not only…but also needs infinitive clothes on both halves, so bare photos is **false** — "…not only to finish the trail but also to edit the photos for the blog."
**E) The workshop taught participants to define goals, to map their route, and to pack a first-aid kit.**

Taught…to introduces three infinitives — define, map, and pack — with to repeated before each outcome. Repeating to keeps each learning goal equally weighted in the workshop list. The series never mixes infinitives with bare nouns or gerunds.

Taught…to with three matching infinitives weights each goal equally, so the workshop wording is **true**.
highlights: bold flavours, neat plating, and generous portions
to define goals, to map their route, and to pack
tasks.solution_overview:
Awareness campaigns, sketchbook applications, chef reputation, trail blogs, and workshop goals. Correlatives fail when one side is a phrase and the other is a clause — or when one side has to and the other does not.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Balance both halves of either…or and not only…but also before you look at meaning. Also watch in + gerund means lists, noun objects after known for, and infinitive teach-lists after taught…to.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cover one correlative half with your finger and check whether the other half could stand in the same grammatical slot. If not, the sentence is false no matter how sensible it sounds.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The contest requires entrants to submit a photo, to write a short caption, and a signed consent form.
Whether by bus, by bike, or on foot, students must reach the hall by nine.
The renovation plan is ambitious, controversial, and it may stall.
She speaks fluently in Spanish, in Italian, and Portuguese.
The app can track sleep, count steps, and remind users to drink water.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The contest requires entrants to submit a photo, to write a short caption, and a signed consent form.**

Requires…to opens an infinitive series with to submit and to write, then ends on a signed consent form with no verb. The last branch is a bare noun, so it cannot sit beside the to-infinitives. Add an infinitive such as to include, or rewrite all three items as nouns after submit.

**Trap:** A consent form is a real contest requirement, so a trailing noun looks deceptively parallel beside two infinitives.

Requires…to can’t end on a bare noun, so the consent form is **false** — "…to submit a photo, to write a short caption, and to include a signed consent form."
**B) Whether by bus, by bike, or on foot, students must reach the hall by nine.**

Whether introduces three prepositional routes — by bus, by bike, or on foot — as matching travel channels. Slight preposition variety (by / on) is fine when every item remains a short prepositional phrase. The route list never switches into a clause or a bare noun.

By bus, by bike, or on foot stay prepositional routes under whether, so the wording is **true**.
**C) The renovation plan is ambitious, controversial, and it may stall.**

Ambitious and controversial are adjectives after is, but it may stall is a clause about risk. Plans described with adjective chains must finish as adjectives, not as freestanding predictions. Use a third adjective so every item remains in the same slot after is.

**Trap:** An it-may-stall clause feels like honest political caution, which hides the adjective-to-clause break.

Plans described with adjectives can’t finish as it may stall, so this is **false** — "The renovation plan is ambitious, controversial, and risky."
**D) She speaks fluently in Spanish, in Italian, and Portuguese.**

In appears before Spanish and Italian but drops before Portuguese. Repeated language markers must either appear on every item or on none. Repeat in before Portuguese, or list all three languages without in.

**Trap:** The last language name looks complete on its own, so a missing shared preposition is a subtle trap.

In before every language (or none) is required, so dropped in is **false** — "…in Spanish, in Italian, and in Portuguese."
**E) The app can track sleep, count steps, and remind users to drink water.**

Can governs three bare infinitives — track, count, and remind — as matching app functions. Shared auxiliaries make parallel verb lists especially clear when every branch stays bare. Nothing adds a stray to or a sudden clause at the end.

Can + track, count, and remind keeps bare app verbs aligned, so the sentence is **true**.

track sleep, count steps, and remind
tasks.solution_overview:
Contest entries, travel routes, renovation politics, language skills, and fitness apps. Missing repeated prepositions and trailing clauses after adjective pairs are the subtler errors here.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Look for infinitive series that end as nouns, whether + preposition route lists, adjective pairs that finish as clauses, language lists that drop in, and bare infinitives after can.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read the list aloud and listen for a change of rhythm. An item that would not fit if it were moved to first position is almost always the parallel break.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The coach argued that fitness was improving, that teamwork was stronger, and morale was high.
She prefers walking in the park to cycle along the busy ring road.
The festival offered live music, outdoor workshops, and free sketching materials.
Not only did they repair the roof, but they also painted the shutters.
His advice was to arrive early, sitting near the aisle, and leave during the interval.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The coach argued that fitness was improving, that teamwork was stronger, and morale was high.**

Argued that opens two that-clauses, then finishes with morale was high missing the repeated that. When that appears twice as a claim marker, the third claim almost always needs it too. Repeat that before morale was high so every claim stays under argued that.

**Trap:** A bare third clause still reports good news, which is why missing that is a classic marker trap.

Argued that needs that on every claim, so missing that is **false** — "…that fitness was improving, that teamwork was stronger, and that morale was high."
**B) She prefers walking in the park to cycle along the busy ring road.**

Prefer A to B needs matching forms on both sides; walking is paired here with cycle. A gerund after prefers must meet another gerund after to, not a bare infinitive. Keep both activities as -ing forms in the comparison.

**Trap:** To cycle looks like a natural travel option beside walking, so the form mismatch after prefer…to is a near-miss.

Prefer A to B wants matching -ing forms, so to cycle is **false** — "She prefers walking in the park to cycling along the busy ring road."
**C) The festival offered live music, outdoor workshops, and free sketching materials.**

Offered takes three noun phrases: live music, outdoor workshops, and free sketching materials. Event programmes list noun objects cleanly when nothing switches to a clause mid-list. Every offering could swap places without changing grammatical shape.

Live music, workshops, and materials all sit as noun offerings, so the programme is **true**.
**D) Not only did they repair the roof, but they also painted the shutters.**

Inverted not only… is balanced by but…also with a parallel past-tense verb phrase (painted the shutters). Both predicates stay finite and matching after the correlative. That mirrored finite structure is what the inversion pattern requires.

Inverted not only…but also mirrors two finite predicates, so the correlative is **true**.
**E) His advice was to arrive early, sitting near the aisle, and leave during the interval.**

Advice opens as an infinitive series (to arrive…, and leave…), but sitting in the middle is a gerund. Middle items must keep the same infinitive clothes when the first and last already use that frame. Use to sit near the aisle so the advice chain never slips into -ing.

**Trap:** Sitting near the aisle feels like natural theatre advice, so a gerund in the middle of an infinitive list is a sharp trap.

Advice framed as infinitives can’t slip into sitting mid-list, so the line is **false** — "…to arrive early, to sit near the aisle, and to leave during the interval."
highlights: live music, outdoor workshops, and free sketching materials
tasks.solution_overview:
Team-talk that-clauses, prefer…to choices, festival offerings, inverted not only…but also, and seating advice. Matching markers must appear on every branch.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Repeated that-clauses need that each time; prefer A to B needs matching forms on both sides; noun festival lists should stay nouns; inverted not only needs a matching finite predicate; infinitive advice chains must not slip into gerunds.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For prefer…to and that-chains, place the first marker beside the last item and ask whether it still fits. Prefer walking… to cycling… (two gerunds) — never walking… to cycle….

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The notice forbids smoking indoors, bringing pets, and to leave bicycles in the hallway.
As much as she loves painting landscapes, she loves photographing them too.
The librarian asked whether the books were returned, whether fines were paid, and cards renewed.
He is neither interested in chess nor in collecting stamps.
To cook well, to plate neatly, and cleaning the kitchen quickly are all part of the shift.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The notice forbids smoking indoors, bringing pets, and to leave bicycles in the hallway.**

Forbids takes gerund objects: smoking and bringing fit, but to leave is an infinitive. Banned actions after forbid/forbids must stay -ing through the last item. Use leaving bicycles in the hallway so every prohibition matches.

**Trap:** To leave bicycles looks like another banned action, which is why an infinitive often sneaks into a gerund ban list.

Forbids takes gerunds, so to leave is **false** — "…smoking indoors, bringing pets, and leaving bicycles in the hallway."
**B) As much as she loves painting landscapes, she loves photographing them too.**

As much as balances two matching loves + gerund clauses: painting landscapes and photographing them. Correlative as much as often needs mirrored verb-plus-complement patterns on both sides. Here both halves keep loves + -ing, so the comparison stays parallel.

As much as mirrors loves + gerund on both sides, so the comparison is **true**.
**C) The librarian asked whether the books were returned, whether fines were paid, and cards renewed.**

Asked whether opens two whether-clauses, then ends on cards renewed without the repeated whether. Checklist branches under whether need the marker on every item, plus a full finite verb if the others have one. Repeat whether and restore were so the third check matches the first two.

**Trap:** A compressed third item still means card renewal, so missing whether is a subtle marker trap.

Asked whether needs the marker (and a full verb) on every check, so cards renewed is **false** — "…whether the books were returned, whether fines were paid, and whether cards were renewed."
**D) He is neither interested in chess nor in collecting stamps.**

Neither…nor joins in chess and in collecting stamps — matching in + noun/gerund phrases after interested. Keeping the same preposition after neither and nor is what balances the hobby pair. Nothing invents a new frame on the second side.

Neither…nor keeps matching in-phrases after interested, so the hobby pair is **true**.
**E) To cook well, to plate neatly, and cleaning the kitchen quickly are all part of the shift.**

To cook and to plate are infinitive subjects, but cleaning the kitchen is a gerund subject. Compound subjects in a duty list must wear one shared form all the way through. Use to clean the kitchen quickly so all three subjects stay infinitives.

**Trap:** Cleaning the kitchen is a real shift duty, so a gerund subject beside two infinitives is a persuasive near-miss.

Compound subjects must share one form, so cleaning among to-infinitives is **false** — "To cook well, to plate neatly, and to clean the kitchen quickly are all part of the shift."
highlights: As much as she loves painting
neither interested in chess nor in collecting
tasks.solution_overview:
Notices, artistic tastes, library checklists, hobbies under neither…nor, and shift duties as subjects. Verb bans, whether-chains, and infinitive subjects look fine until the last item switches form.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Treat the first branch as a template: gerunds after forbids, mirrored loves + gerund under as much as, whether repeated on every checklist item, matching in-phrases after neither…nor, and all-infinitive compound subjects.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Force every later branch to copy the first. If you see forbids… -ing, -ing, to… or to…, to…, -ing as a subject list, mark false immediately.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The brochure promises clearer maps, shorter queues, and that tickets will be refundable.
Whether to reschedule the match, whether to move indoors, or cancelling altogether was debated for hours.
She left early because of a headache, because of the noise, and because her phone battery had died.
The trainer emphasised warming up properly, cooling down slowly, and drinking enough water.
His reply was polite, brief, and unexpectedly helpful.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The brochure promises clearer maps, shorter queues, and that tickets will be refundable.**

Clearer maps and shorter queues are noun phrases, but that tickets will be refundable is a that-clause. Brochure promises listed as nouns cannot suddenly finish as a full that-clause. Recast the last promise as a noun phrase so all three stay in one frame.

**Trap:** A refundability that-clause feels like another visitor benefit, which hides the noun-to-clause switch.

Noun promises can’t finish as a that-clause, so refundability is **false** — "…clearer maps, shorter queues, and refundable tickets."
**B) Whether to reschedule the match, whether to move indoors, or cancelling altogether was debated for hours.**

Two options open as whether to + infinitive, but cancelling altogether is a gerund. Debate options under whether to must keep that marker and infinitive form on every alternative. Write whether to cancel altogether so the third option matches the first two.

**Trap:** Cancelling altogether is a real debate option, so a bare gerund after two whether-to phrases is a classic trap.

Whether to chains must stay infinitive, so cancelling is **false** — "…whether to reschedule the match, whether to move indoors, or whether to cancel altogether…."
**C) She left early because of a headache, because of the noise, and because her phone battery had died.**

Two reasons open as because of + noun phrases, but because her phone battery had died is a because-clause. Because of and because are different scaffolds; mixing them mid-list breaks parallelism. Rewrite the last reason as because of + noun, or rewrite all three as because-clauses.

**Trap:** A dead-battery because-clause still names a genuine reason, which makes the because of / because clash easy to miss.

Because of and because are different scaffolds, so the mixed reasons fail — "…because of a headache, because of the noise, and because of a dead phone battery."
**D) The trainer emphasised warming up properly, cooling down slowly, and drinking enough water.**

Emphasised takes three gerund phrases — warming up, cooling down, and drinking — with matching complements. Long gerund objects remain correct when every item is -ing plus its complement. The training list never slips into an infinitive or a clause.

Warming up, cooling down, and drinking stay -ing after emphasised, so the training list is **true**.
**E) His reply was polite, brief, and unexpectedly helpful.**

Was is followed by three adjectives — polite, brief, and unexpectedly helpful. An adverb such as unexpectedly can modify an adjective without breaking the adjective chain. Every item still occupies the same descriptive slot after was.

Polite, brief, and unexpectedly helpful remain adjectives after was, so the wording is **true**.
highlights: and that tickets will be refundable
warming up properly, cooling down slowly, and drinking
tasks.solution_overview:
Brochure promises, indoor/outdoor debates, mixed reason frames, training emphasis, and a helpful reply. Mid-band items mix noun lists with whether-to chains and because of / because clashes.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Pick one frame — nouns, whether to, because of, gerunds after emphasised, or adjectives after was — and hold it through every item. Mixing a that-clause into a noun list, or a gerund into a whether-to chain, is the classic fail.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Write the first item's frame in the margin, then rewrite the last item mentally using that same frame. If the rewrite needs a different scaffold, the original sentence is false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Success on the course depended not so much on raw talent as practising every evening.
The neighbours debated whether to plant hedges, whether to build a fence, or installing a gate.
House rules forbid leaving dishes overnight, borrowing tools without asking, and using the roof terrace after midnight.
Her weekend is as much about cooking for friends as it is about catching up on sleep.
The motion was neither seconded promptly nor was it discussed on the merits.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Success on the course depended not so much on raw talent as practising every evening.**

Not so much…as joins on raw talent to practising every evening without repeating on. Comparative frames that open with a preposition almost always need that same preposition on the second half. Repeat on before the gerund so both sides share one scaffold.

**Trap:** Practising every evening is the real point of contrast, so a dropped on after as is a high-band near-miss.

Not so much…as that opens with on needs on again, so practising alone is **false** — "…not so much on raw talent as on practising every evening."
**B) The neighbours debated whether to plant hedges, whether to build a fence, or installing a gate.**

Two alternatives open as whether to + infinitive, but installing a gate is a gerund. Neighbourhood options under whether to must keep that marker and infinitive form throughout. Write whether to install a gate so every alternative matches.

**Trap:** Installing a gate is a plausible third option, which is why a bare gerund after whether-to phrases is a sharp trap.

Whether to options can’t end as a bare gerund, so installing is **false** — "…whether to plant hedges, whether to build a fence, or whether to install a gate."
**C) House rules forbid leaving dishes overnight, borrowing tools without asking, and using the roof terrace after midnight.**

Forbid takes three gerund phrases — leaving, borrowing, and using — with matching complements. House-rule bans stay parallel when every prohibited action is -ing plus its details. Nothing switches into a noun, infinitive, or clause at the end.

Leaving, borrowing, and using keep -ing bans after forbid, so the house rules stand.
**D) Her weekend is as much about cooking for friends as it is about catching up on sleep.**

As much…as balances two about + gerund ideas with matching it is: about cooking… and about catching up…. Correlative as much…as often needs mirrored about-phrases on both sides. Here both halves keep the same about + gerund scaffold.

As much…as mirrors about + gerund on both weekend halves, so the pair is **true**.
**E) The motion was neither seconded promptly nor was it discussed on the merits.**

Neither…nor joins seconded promptly (a past-participle phrase) to was it discussed… (an inverted finite clause). After a passive was, both correlative halves should stay past participles, not flip into inversion after nor. Keep neither seconded… nor discussed… without was it.

**Trap:** Nor was it discussed looks polished and formal, so the inverted clause after neither…nor is a high-band trap.

Neither…nor after was wants past participles, so inverted was it is **false** — "The motion was neither seconded promptly nor discussed on the merits."
highlights: leaving dishes overnight, borrowing tools without asking, and using
as much about cooking for friends as it is about
tasks.solution_overview:
Advanced correlatives — not so much…as, whether to…, as much…as, neither…nor — plus a clean house-rules gerund list. Match the scaffolding, not just the topic.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

These frames fail when the second half drops a preposition, switches from whether to + infinitive to a bare gerund, or flips from a past participle into an inverted finite clause after nor.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Align the prepositions and verb forms first; only then ask whether the ideas belong together. A matching topic with mismatched scaffolding is still false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The flyer promises visitors free entry, guided tours, and that parking will be available nearby.
By labelling drawers clearly, by colour-coding folders, and by clearing the desk nightly, she found her keys faster.
The candidate was praised for how she handled questions, how she framed answers, and her closing thank-you.
We will either finish the quilt this weekend or postpone the sewing circle until Friday.
The rule requires that guests sign in, that they leave keys at reception, and bikes be locked outside.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The flyer promises visitors free entry, guided tours, and that parking will be available nearby.**

Free entry and guided tours are noun phrases, but that parking will be available nearby is a that-clause. Flyer promises listed as nouns cannot finish as a full that-clause. Recast parking as a noun phrase so all three visitor perks match.

**Trap:** A parking that-clause still promises a real amenity, which hides the noun-to-clause switch.

Flyer perks listed as nouns can’t end as a that-clause, so this is **false** — "…free entry, guided tours, and nearby parking."
**B) By labelling drawers clearly, by colour-coding folders, and by clearing the desk nightly, she found her keys faster.**

Three matching by + gerund phrases — labelling, colour-coding, and clearing — list the means that sped up the search. Repeating by before each gerund keeps the causal list balanced and easy to hear. That repeated marker is what locks the parallel pattern.

Three by + gerund means phrases share one causal scaffold, so the wording is **true**.
**C) The candidate was praised for how she handled questions, how she framed answers, and her closing thank-you.**

Two praises open as how-clauses, but her closing thank-you is a bare noun phrase. Interview praise under how must keep that how-frame on every branch. Add how she delivered her closing thank-you so the third item matches.

**Trap:** A thank-you noun looks like another praised moment, so the dropped how is a persuasive near-miss.

How-clause praise needs how on every branch, so her closing thank-you is **false** — "…how she handled questions, how she framed answers, and how she delivered her closing thank-you."
**D) We will either finish the quilt this weekend or postpone the sewing circle until Friday.**

Either…or joins finish… and postpone… — two matching bare infinitives after will. Shared will plus either…or needs the same bare verb form on both sides. Nothing invents a new subject or slips into a different verb shape.

Will either…or balances finish and postpone as bare infinitives, so the plan is **true**.
**E) The rule requires that guests sign in, that they leave keys at reception, and bikes be locked outside.**

Requires that opens two that-clauses, then ends on bikes be locked outside without the repeated that. House rules stacked under that need the marker on every requirement. Repeat that before the bike rule so the third clause matches the first two.

**Trap:** A compressed final rule still sounds official, which is why missing that is a high-band marker trap.

Requires that needs that on every rule, so bikes be locked is **false** — "…that guests sign in, that they leave keys at reception, and that bikes be locked outside."
highlights: and that parking will be available
By labelling drawers clearly, by colour-coding
either finish the quilt this weekend or postpone
tasks.solution_overview:
Flyer language, drawer-labelling means lists, interview praise, quilt plans, and reception rules. Flyer promises and house rules often stack that-clauses.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If that appears twice, the third clause almost always needs it too — or rewrite all three as nouns. Also watch by + gerund means lists, how-clause praise chains, and either…or after will.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Count the repeated markers (by, how, that, either/or). Any branch that lacks the shared marker while the others keep it is the break in parallelism.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The strategy rests less on expensive kit than practising basic drills.
Not only did attendance rise in spring, but energy levels also improved.
Readers asked for a guide that is clear, that is illustrated, and useful without jargon.
The club prefers meeting outdoors on Saturdays and to convene indoors on rainy Sundays.
A solid packing list must specify what to wear, what to carry, and when to leave.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The strategy rests less on expensive kit than practising basic drills.**

Less…than joins on expensive kit to practising basic drills without repeating on. Comparative frames that open with a preposition need that same preposition after than. Write than on practising so both sides share one scaffold.

**Trap:** Practising basic drills is the intended contrast, so a dropped on after than is a classic high-band trap.

Less…than that opens with on needs on after than, so practising alone is **false** — "…less on expensive kit than on practising basic drills."
**B) Not only did attendance rise in spring, but energy levels also improved.**

Inverted not only… is balanced by but…also with a parallel past-tense predicate (energy levels also improved). Both sides stay finite and matching after the correlative. That mirrored finite structure is what the inversion pattern requires.

Inverted not only…but also mirrors two past-tense rises, so the correlative is **true**.
**C) Readers asked for a guide that is clear, that is illustrated, and useful without jargon.**

Two relative modifiers open with that is, but useful without jargon stands alone. Either finish the relative chain with that is useful…, or drop that is before every adjective. Partial repetition of that is is what breaks the guide description.

**Trap:** Useful without jargon looks like a third quality already, so missing that is is easy to miss.

That is on two adjectives leaves the third bare, so useful is **false** — "…that is clear, that is illustrated, and that is useful without jargon."
**D) The club prefers meeting outdoors on Saturdays and to convene indoors on rainy Sundays.**

Meeting (a gerund) is paired with to convene (an infinitive) after prefers. Prefer needs matching gerunds or matching infinitives on both days — not one of each. Pick one form and use it for Saturday and Sunday alike.

**Trap:** Indoor convening on rainy Sundays is a real alternative, so mixed -ing / to forms after prefers is a near-miss.

Prefer can’t pair a gerund with an infinitive, so the club days fail — "…meeting outdoors… and convening indoors…" or "to meet… and to convene…."
**E) A solid packing list must specify what to wear, what to carry, and when to leave.**

Must specify introduces three matching wh-infinitive phrases: what to wear, what to carry, and when to leave. Parallel wh-phrases are ideal when a packing list must answer what and when in the same frame. Every branch keeps the wh + to + verb shape.

What to wear, what to carry, and when to leave share one wh-infinitive frame, so the packing cue is **true**.
highlights: what to wear, what to carry, and when to leave
tasks.solution_overview:
Comparative frames (less…than), inverted not only…but also, relative-clause chains, prefer + mixed forms, and wh-infinitive packing lists. Demand the same marker on every branch.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Less…than needs a matching preposition on both sides; that is relatives need that is on every adjective (or on none); prefer needs matching gerunds or matching infinitives; wh-infinitives should stay in the what/when frame.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

When in doubt, rewrite the last item so it could replace the first without changing structure. If you need a new marker to make that swap, the sentence is false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The flatshare rules cover quiet hours, shared cleaning, and guests must leave by eleven.
She trains both in the gym and when the weather allows outdoor runs.
The quiz tracked page views, session duration, and how long users stayed on each question.
To attract volunteers, to retain helpers, and to protect their time are shared priorities.
The teacher advised against skipping warm-ups, against ignoring form, and against rushing the last set.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The flatshare rules cover quiet hours, shared cleaning, and guests must leave by eleven.**

Quiet hours and shared cleaning are noun objects after cover, but guests must leave by eleven is an independent clause. House-rule lists written as nouns cannot finish as freestanding rules with new verbs. Recast the guest curfew as a noun phrase so every covered item matches.

**Trap:** An eleven o'clock guest rule feels like another flatshare policy, which hides the noun-to-clause switch.

Cover takes noun objects, so a guests-must clause is **false** — "…quiet hours, shared cleaning, and an eleven o'clock guest curfew."
**B) She trains both in the gym and when the weather allows outdoor runs.**

Both…and joins in the gym (a prepositional phrase) to when the weather allows outdoor runs (a when-clause). Correlative halves must share the same category of place/time phrase, not merely related training scenes. Rewrite the second half as a matching prepositional phrase.

**Trap:** A when-clause about outdoor runs still describes training conditions, so the category switch after both…and is a sharp trap.

Both…and needs matching place phrases, so a when-clause is **false** — "She trains both in the gym and in the park."
**C) The quiz tracked page views, session duration, and how long users stayed on each question.**

Page views and session duration are noun metrics, but how long users stayed… is a how-clause. Quiz analytics listed as nouns cannot suddenly finish as a free how-clause. Recast the last metric as a noun phrase so all three measurements match.

**Trap:** A how-long clause still reports dwell time, which is why the noun-to-clause mix looks plausible.

Quiz metrics listed as nouns can’t finish as a how-clause, so the line is **false** — "…page views, session duration, and question dwell time."
**D) To attract volunteers, to retain helpers, and to protect their time are shared priorities.**

Three infinitive phrases — to attract, to retain, and to protect — function as a parallel compound subject. Infinitive subjects stay parallel when every infinitive carries the same role in the sentence. Nothing slips into a gerund or a bare noun as a fourth-looking subject.

To attract, to retain, and to protect all work as infinitive subjects, so the priorities hold.
**E) The teacher advised against skipping warm-ups, against ignoring form, and against rushing the last set.**

Advised against opens three matching against + gerund phrases for the warning list. Repeating against before each gerund locks the parallel pattern. Every caution stays inside the same preposition-plus-gerund frame.

Repeating against + gerund locks each caution in one frame, so the warning list is **true**.
highlights: and guests must leave by eleven
both in the gym and when
To attract volunteers, to retain helpers, and to protect
against skipping warm-ups, against ignoring form, and against rushing
tasks.solution_overview:
Flatshare rules, gym-versus-weather training, quiz metrics, volunteer priorities as infinitive subjects, and coach warnings with against + gerund. Drafts mix nouns, infinitives, and clauses freely — you must refuse that mixing.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Pick one frame and hold it: all nouns for house-rule objects, matching prepositional phrases after both…and, all noun metrics (not a how-clause), all infinitive subjects, or all against + gerund warnings.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cover the last item and ask whether it could be item one in the same grammatical clothes. Clauses after noun objects, and when-clauses after in the gym, fail that test.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

As much…as mirrors about + gerund for trust and sleep alike, so the weekend comparison is **true**.
**E) The complaint was neither acknowledged promptly nor was it investigated in full.**

Neither…nor joins acknowledged promptly (a past-participle phrase) to was it investigated… (an inverted finite clause). After a passive was, both correlative halves should remain past participles. Drop the inverted was it and keep neither acknowledged… nor investigated….

**Trap:** Nor was it investigated sounds formally balanced, so the inversion after neither…nor is a high-band trap.

Neither…nor after was wants past participles, so nor was it investigated is **false** — "The complaint was neither acknowledged promptly nor investigated in full."
highlights: accepting strangers' parcels, soliciting room swaps, and using
as much about rebuilding trust with neighbours as it is about
tasks.solution_overview:
Recovery plans, race-day debates, hostel bans, neighbour trust, and complaint handling — all under advanced correlatives. Dropped prepositions and verb-form switches are the high-band traps.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Not so much…as needs on on both sides; whether to chains must not end in a bare gerund; forbid + gerund lists must stay -ing; as much…as needs mirrored about-phrases; neither…nor must not flip into was it… after nor.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Match the scaffolding first. A second half that only rhymes thematically with the first half still fails if the preposition or verb form has changed.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival flyer promises clearer maps, shorter queues, and that shuttle buses will run until midnight.
By training marshals early, by publishing diversion signs, and by checking radios hourly, the walk reduced delays.
The speaker was praised for how she handled hecklers, how she timed jokes, and her encore story.
We will either finish the scrapbook this year or postpone the project until spring.
The campsite asks that visitors log arrivals, that they sort recycling carefully, and fires be extinguished by ten.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The festival flyer promises clearer maps, shorter queues, and that shuttle buses will run until midnight.**

Clearer maps and shorter queues are noun phrases, but that shuttle buses will run until midnight is a that-clause. Festival promises listed as nouns cannot finish as a full that-clause. Recast the shuttle offer as a noun phrase so all three promises match.

**Trap:** A midnight-shuttle that-clause still sells a real amenity, which hides the noun-to-clause break.

Noun festival promises can’t finish as a that-clause, so shuttle buses don’t hold — "…clearer maps, shorter queues, and midnight shuttle buses."
**B) By training marshals early, by publishing diversion signs, and by checking radios hourly, the walk reduced delays.**

Three matching by + gerund phrases — training, publishing, and checking — list the means that reduced delays. Repeating by before each gerund keeps the causal scaffold balanced. That repeated marker locks the parallel pattern for the walk's logistics.

Training, publishing, and checking all sit under by + gerund, so the logistics wording is **true**.
**C) The speaker was praised for how she handled hecklers, how she timed jokes, and her encore story.**

Two praises open as how-clauses, but her encore story is a bare noun phrase. Stage praise under how must keep that how-frame on every branch. Add how she delivered her encore story so the third item matches.

**Trap:** An encore-story noun looks like another praised moment, so the dropped how is a persuasive near-miss.

How-clause praise needs how throughout, so her encore story is **false** — "…how she handled hecklers, how she timed jokes, and how she delivered her encore story."
**D) We will either finish the scrapbook this year or postpone the project until spring.**

Either…or joins finish… and postpone… — two matching bare infinitives after will. Shared will plus either…or needs the same bare verb form on both sides. The scrapbook plan never invents a new subject or a different verb shape.

Either…or after will pairs finish and postpone as bare infinitives, so the scrapbook plan is **true**.
**E) The campsite asks that visitors log arrivals, that they sort recycling carefully, and fires be extinguished by ten.**

Asks that opens two that-clauses, then ends on fires be extinguished by ten without the repeated that. Campsite rules stacked under that need the marker on every requirement. Repeat that before the fire rule so the third clause matches.

**Trap:** A compressed fire-extinguish rule still sounds official, so missing that is a top-band marker trap.

Asks that needs that on every campsite rule, so fires be extinguished is **false** — "…that visitors log arrivals, that they sort recycling carefully, and that fires be extinguished by ten."
highlights: and that shuttle buses will run
By training marshals early, by publishing
either finish the scrapbook this year or postpone
tasks.solution_overview:
Festival flyers, marshal training, stage praise, scrapbook deadlines, and campsite rules. Stacked that-clauses and how-chains are the recurring exams traps at this band.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If that appears twice, the third clause needs it too — or rewrite all three as nouns. Keep by + gerund means lists, how-clause praise chains, either…or after will, and campsite that-rules in one consistent frame.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Count repeated markers (by, how, that). Any final branch that sheds the marker while the first branches keep it is parallel failure.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Good bread rests less on exotic flour than kneading the dough with patience.
Not only did attendance rise after Easter, but energy levels also improved.
Campers asked for a trail note that is realistic, that is waterproof, and useful without jargon.
The choir prefers rehearsing in person on Mondays and to rehearse online on Thursdays.
A solid itinerary must specify who books the tickets, what bags are allowed, and when the group will meet.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Good bread rests less on exotic flour than kneading the dough with patience.**

Less…than joins on exotic flour to kneading the dough without repeating on. Comparative frames that open with a preposition need that same preposition after than. Write than on kneading so both sides share one scaffold.

**Trap:** Kneading with patience is the intended contrast, so a dropped on after than is a classic high-band trap.

Less…than that opens with on needs on again, so kneading alone is **false** — "…less on exotic flour than on kneading the dough with patience."
**B) Not only did attendance rise after Easter, but energy levels also improved.**

Inverted not only… is balanced by but…also with a parallel past-tense predicate (energy levels also improved). Both sides stay finite and matching after the correlative. That mirrored finite structure is what the inversion pattern requires.

Inverted not only…but also balances two finite improvements, so the wording is **true**.
**C) Campers asked for a trail note that is realistic, that is waterproof, and useful without jargon.**

Two relative modifiers open with that is, but useful without jargon stands alone. Finish the relative chain with that is useful…, or drop that is before every adjective. Partial repetition of that is breaks the trail-note description.

**Trap:** Useful without jargon looks ready-made as a third quality, so missing that is is easy to overlook.

That is repeated twice leaves useful bare, so this is **false** — "…that is realistic, that is waterproof, and that is useful without jargon."
**D) The choir prefers rehearsing in person on Mondays and to rehearse online on Thursdays.**

Rehearsing (a gerund) is paired with to rehearse (an infinitive) after prefers. Prefer needs matching gerunds or matching infinitives for both rehearsal days. Pick one form and keep it for Mondays and Thursdays alike.

**Trap:** Online rehearsal on Thursdays is a real alternative, so mixed -ing / to forms after prefers is a near-miss.

Prefer needs one shared form for both rehearsal days, so the mixed pair is **false** — "…rehearsing in person… and rehearsing online…" or "to rehearse… and to rehearse…."
**E) A solid itinerary must specify who books the tickets, what bags are allowed, and when the group will meet.**

Must specify introduces three matching wh-clauses: who books…, what bags…, and when the group will meet. Parallel wh-clauses are ideal when an itinerary must answer ownership, contents, and timing together. Every branch keeps a full wh + finite-clause shape.

Who / what / when clauses under must specify stay parallel, so the itinerary frame is **true**.
highlights: who books the tickets, what bags
tasks.solution_overview:
Bread science, post-Easter attendance, trail notes, choir rehearsal modes, and itinerary wh-clauses. Comparative frames and relative-clause chains still demand matching markers.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Less…than needs on on both sides; inverted not only needs matching finite predicates; that is relatives need that is on every adjective (or none); prefer needs matching forms; wh-clauses should stay who / what / when in parallel.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Rewrite the last item so it could replace the first without changing structure. That mental swap exposes dropped prepositions, missing that is, and mixed -ing / to forms.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The landlord authorised tenants to repaint the hallway, to replace the hallway bulbs, and filing a repair request if leaks returned.
Just as the café invests in better beans, so too does it invest in staff training.
Progress will be judged on whether chores are finished, whether keys are returned, and communal lights are off.
The brief is neither to defend every habit nor to dismiss every suggestion wholesale.
She moved out because of limited daylight, because of noisy neighbours, and her commute had become unmanageable.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The landlord authorised tenants to repaint the hallway, to replace the hallway bulbs, and filing a repair request if leaks returned.**

Authorised…to opens an infinitive series with to repaint and to replace, but filing is a gerund. Permissions after authorised to must stay infinitives through the last allowed action. Use to file a repair request so the series never changes form.

**Trap:** Filing a repair request is a real allowed action, so a gerund at the end of a to-series is a top-band near-miss.

Authorised…to needs infinitives throughout, so filing is **false** — "…to repaint the hallway, to replace the hallway bulbs, and to file a repair request if leaks returned."
**B) Just as the café invests in better beans, so too does it invest in staff training.**

Just as…so too balances two matching invest + in + noun patterns, with inversion on the second clause. Correlative just as…so too needs mirrored clause structure on both sides. Here both halves keep invest in + noun, so the café comparison stays parallel.

Just as…so too mirrors invest + in on both café sides, so the correlative is **true**.
**C) Progress will be judged on whether chores are finished, whether keys are returned, and communal lights are off.**

Judged on whether opens two whether-clauses, then ends on communal lights are off without the repeated whether. Progress checklists under whether need the marker on every criterion. Repeat whether before the lights clause so the third check matches.

**Trap:** A bare lights-are-off clause still names a real progress test, so missing whether is a high-band marker trap.

Judged on whether needs whether on every criterion, so lights are off is **false** — "…whether chores are finished, whether keys are returned, and whether communal lights are off."
**D) The brief is neither to defend every habit nor to dismiss every suggestion wholesale.**

Neither…nor joins to defend… and to dismiss… — two matching infinitives after is. Keep to + bare verb on both sides of neither…nor so the brief stays balanced. Nothing drops to or flips into a finite clause on the second half.

Neither…nor joins two matching to-infinitives after is, so the brief is **true**.
**E) She moved out because of limited daylight, because of noisy neighbours, and her commute had become unmanageable.**

Two reasons open as because of + noun phrases, but her commute had become unmanageable is an independent clause. Once because of sets the frame, every later reason should stay a noun phrase under that marker. Recast the commute as because of + noun so all three reasons match.

**Trap:** A freestanding commute clause still states a genuine motive, which hides the because of / clause switch.

Because of sets noun reasons the commute clause leaves, so this is **false** — "…because of limited daylight, because of noisy neighbours, and because of an unmanageable commute."
highlights: neither to defend every habit nor to dismiss
tasks.solution_overview:
Final-band mix: long infinitive authorisations, just as…so too correlatives, whether-progress checklists, neither…nor briefings, and because of reason chains. Name the opening structure, then reject any ending that cannot wear the same grammatical clothes.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Combined traps here are authorised…to lists that end in gerunds, whether-chains missing the third whether, because of pairs that finish as independent clauses, and (correct) mirrored just as…so too / neither…nor infinitive pairs.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For every sentence, write the first branch's structure in one word — infinitive, whether-clause, because of + noun, invest + in — and demand that label for every later branch.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE
